{{Short description|Family of probability distributions}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Gaussian ''q''-distribution}}
{{About|the distribution introduced by Diaz and Teruel|the Tsallis q-Gaussian|q-Gaussian}}

In [[mathematical physics]] and [[probability]] and [[statistics]], the '''Gaussian ''q''-distribution''' is a family of [[probability distribution]]s that includes, as [[limiting case (mathematics)|limiting case]]s, the [[uniform distribution (continuous)|uniform distribution]] and the [[Normal distribution|normal (Gaussian) distribution]]. It was introduced by Diaz and Teruel.{{Clarify|reason=literature suggests that others originated this|date=August 2011}} It is a [[q-analog]] of the Gaussian or [[normal distribution]].

The distribution is symmetric about zero and is bounded, except for the limiting case of the normal distribution. The limiting uniform distribution is on the range -1 to +1.

==Definition==
[[Image:Gaussianq-density2.jpg|thumb|500px|The Gaussian q-density.]]

Let ''q'' be a [[real number]] in the interval [0,&nbsp;1). The [[probability density function]] of the  Gaussian ''q''-distribution is given by

:<math>s_q(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if }  x < -\nu  \\ \frac{1}{c(q)}E_{q^2}^{\frac{-q^2x^2}{[2]_q}}  & \text{if } -\nu \leq x \leq \nu \\ 0 & \mbox{if } x >\nu. \end{cases} </math>

where

:<math>\nu = \nu(q) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-q}} ,</math>

: <math>c(q)=2(1-q)^{1/2}\sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^m q^{m(m+1)}}{(1-q^{2m+1})(1-q^2)_{q^2}^m} .</math>

The ''q''-analogue [''t'']<sub>''q''</sub> of the real number <math> t </math> is given by

: <math> [t]_q=\frac{q^t-1}{q-1}. </math>

The ''q''-analogue of the [[exponential function]] is the [[q-exponential]], ''E''{{su|b=''q''|p=''x''}}, which is given by

: <math> E_q^{x}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^{j(j-1)/2}\frac{x^{j}}{[j]!}</math>

where the ''q''-analogue of the [[factorial]] is the [[q-factorial]], [''n'']<sub>''q''</sub>!, which is in turn given by

: <math> [n]_q!=[n]_q[n-1]_q\cdots [2]_q \, </math>

for an integer ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2 and [1]<sub>''q''</sub>! =&nbsp;[0]<sub>''q''</sub>!&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.

[[Image:CumulativeGaussianq-distribution2.jpg|thumb|500px|The Cumulative Gaussian q-distribution.]]

The [[cumulative distribution function]] of the Gaussian ''q''-distribution is given by

: <math>G_q(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x < -\nu \\[12pt]
\displaystyle \frac{1}{c(q)}\int_{-\nu}^{x} E_{q^2}^{-q^2 t^2/[2]} \, d_qt & \text{if }  -\nu \leq x \leq \nu \\[12pt]
1 & \text{if } x>\nu
\end{cases}</math>

where the [[integral|integration]] symbol denotes the [[Jackson integral]].

The function ''G''<sub>''q''</sub> is given explicitly by

: <math>G_q(x)= \begin{cases}  0 & \text{if } x < -\nu, \\
\displaystyle \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1-q}{c(q)} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{q^{n(n+1)}(q-1)^n}{(1-q^{2n+1})(1-q^2)_{q^2}^{n}}x^{2n+1} &  \text{if } -\nu \leq x \leq \nu \\
1 & \text{if}\ x > \nu
\end{cases}</math>

where

: <math>(a+b)_q^n=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(a+q^ib) .</math>

==Moments==
The [[moment (mathematics)|moment]]s of the Gaussian ''q''-distribution are given by

: <math>\frac{1}{c(q)}\int_{-\nu}^\nu E_{q^2}^{-q^2 x^2/[2]} \, x^{2n} \, d_qx =[2n-1]!! ,</math>

: <math>\frac{1}{c(q)}\int_{-\nu}^\nu E_{q^{2}}^{-q^2 x^2/[2]} \, x^{2n+1} \, d_qx=0 ,</math>

where the symbol [2''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1]<nowiki>!!</nowiki> is the ''q''-analogue of the [[double factorial]] given by

: <math> [2n-1][2n-3]\cdots[1]= [2n-1]!!. \, </math>
